analysis.one_liner: Creates a USDA competition enforcer and bans unfair contracting practices against livestock and poultry farmers.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in February 2006 with bipartisan sponsorship but never received a committee vote or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set up a new office inside the Agriculture Department dedicated to investigating and prosecuting unfair practices by big livestock dealers, meat processors, and agricultural contractors. It would have banned unfair or deceptive practices in agricultural contracts, let contract farmers cancel some contracts, required large agribusiness firms to disclose their corporate structure, and made it easier for farmers to win cases by removing the requirement to prove that a company's conduct actually hurt competition. It also extended existing livestock-market rules to cover live poultry dealers for the first time.
analysis.who_benefits: Family farmers, ranchers, and especially contract growers — the poultry and hog producers who raise animals under contracts with large companies. The bill would give them the right to cancel certain contracts within three business days, place a legal lien on the animals and proceeds they produce so they get paid first if a contractor goes broke, require plain-language disclosure of key contract terms, bar companies from forcing producers into one-sided confidentiality and arbitration clauses, and require 180 days' notice before a company cancels a contract that required a producer to invest $100,000 or more. It would also let producers sue and recover damages and attorney's fees without having to prove the company's conduct injured competition.

how_it_helps.text: Creates an Office of Special Counsel for Competition Matters at USDA to investigate and prosecute violations of the Packers and Stockyards Act and other competition laws, with a Senate-confirmed head and its own lawyers.

Makes unfair or deceptive acts in agricultural commerce, contracts, and dealings with producer associations unlawful, and eliminates the requirement that farmers prove competitive injury or predatory intent to prevail.

Gives contract producers a lien on the commodity and its sale proceeds, superior to other creditors' claims, plus a three-business-day cancellation right and mandatory disclosure of key contract terms.

Voids contract confidentiality requirements (except true trade secrets), lets farmers choose whether to arbitrate a dispute after it arises, and voids clauses applying another state's law or moving the case out of the farmer's home state.

Extends Packers and Stockyards Act enforcement to live poultry dealers by removing the slaughter requirement from the definitions, and authorizes temporary injunctions in cases involving poultry care.

analysis.who_pays: Large agricultural contractors, meatpackers, processors, and live poultry dealers — companies with more than $100 million in annual sales would have to file annual reports on their subsidiaries, joint ventures, and interlocking boards, and all covered firms would face new lawsuit exposure, attorney's-fee awards to prevailing farmers, and restrictions on how they write and terminate production contracts.

drawbacks.text: Restrictions on termination and on requiring producers to make capital investments could make large contractors more cautious about offering production contracts at all, potentially reducing opportunities for growers even as it protects existing ones.

Letting a farmer win without proving competitive injury lowers the burden of proof considerably and could expose companies to litigation over ordinary business practices, a cost that could ultimately be passed through the food chain.
The new USDA enforcement office and the 180-day rulemaking mandate would expand the Department's regulatory reach across the entire agricultural marketing chain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the farmers who raise livestock and poultry under contract, the protections — payment liens, cancellation rights, notice before termination, and an easier legal standard — are substantial and directly targeted at documented bargaining-imbalance problems in contract agriculture. The main costs fall on the large contractors and processors, and some of those costs (litigation risk, more cautious contracting) could trickle down to growers and consumers; on balance the bill was aimed squarely at rebalancing power away from concentrated agribusiness toward individual producers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Harkin introduced the bill on February 16, 2006, together with Sens. Enzi and Thomas, both Republicans.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry on the day of introduction.
The committee took no further action — no hearings, markup, or floor vote appear in the action history — and the bill expired with the end of the 109th Congress on January 3, 2007.

The bill would have required agribusiness firms with over $100 million in annual sales to report their corporate structure annually and created a dedicated USDA office to prosecute unfair agricultural trade practices.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large livestock dealers, meatpackers, poultry integrators, and agricultural contractors are better off, because they face none of the new reporting duties, contract restrictions, or lawsuit exposure the bill would have imposed. Contract farmers gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor and three Republican cosponsors, but the Republican-chaired Agriculture Committee never acted on it, so no vote ever revealed where the parties stood.

industries.note: The bill would have exposed packers to suit without any showing of competitive injury, forced annual disclosure of corporate structure, and barred most volume-based price preferences. These are companies whose market power over cattle and hog sellers was the bill's central target.

industries.industry: Poultry integrators and live poultry dealers
industries.note: Removing the slaughter requirement would have brought live poultry dealers under Packers and Stockyards Act enforcement for the first time, and growers would no longer have to prove competitive injury. This industry contracts with thousands of small growers who currently bear the investment risk.

New disclosure rules, voided confidentiality and forced-arbitration clauses, producer liens, and cancellation rights would have shifted bargaining power toward producers and raised legal costs for contractors.

Cooperatives would be subject to the unfair-practices rules but are exempted from the producer-lien requirement when producers hold at least half the ownership, and Capper-Volstead cooperatives are carved out of the processor definition.
